title: TA7-06359
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, the claimant, seeks refugee protection under ss 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). All of the evidence submitted and counsel's submissions and the Tribunal Officer's representations were received and carefully considered. Decision

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee because he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in United Arab Emirates, his country of former habitual residence, if he were to return. I also find that the claimant is not a person in need of protection, in that his removal to United Arab Emirates would not subject him personally to a risk to his life, or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to United Arab Emirates will subject him personally to a danger of torture. Allegations

The following is a summary of the claimant's allegations from the narrative of his second Personal Information Form (PIF).1 He alleged his claim should be heard against Lebanon, since he has a travel document from that country.

The claimant said his life was very comfortable in United Arab Emirates until XXXXX XXXXX, 2007, when his best friend, XXXXX XXXXX - XXXXX, a stateless Palestinian, was arrested by state security. The claimant said he has heard nothing of his friend since that day. He said he was questioned by state security, three times, regarding his friend and whether his friend was a member of Hamas. He said he noticed that he was under surveillance and his family suggested he go to Canada because his life might be at risk.
The claimant said he has no rights in UAE and cannot stay there without a sponsor. He came to Canada on XXXXX XXXXX, 2007 and made his claim the same day.

The claimant's first narrative2 does not mention any problems in United Arab Emirates. He said his first lawyer would not permit this to be included in his narrative. The first narrative said his residency permit for UAE expired on XXXXX XXXXX, 2007. He said his father had been laid off the previous XXXXX, and that, as a stateless descendant of a Palestinian family, he would have to live in a refugee camp there and his human rights would be violated and he would be killed. Identity
The claimant's personal identity is established by his travel document3 and birth certificate.4 I find that the claimant has established his personal identity.

The claimant's nationality or citizenship is complicated. The claimant was born in and lived his whole life in United Arab Emirates. He said his father left the refugee camp in Lebanon, where the whole family lived, on XXXXX XXXXX, 1972 and went to XXXXX XXXXX to seek employment. The claimant's father married his mother there and he and all his siblings were born in UAE.

The question of his citizenship, or lack thereof, requires further analysis. The claimant came to Canada using a Lebanese document.5 It expired on XXXXX XXXXX 2009 before the claim was scheduled to be heard. The claimant said he is a stateless Palestinian.

Although the claimant's father came from Lebanon, he was not a citizen there and was a refugee living in a refugee camp. The Lebanon Citizenship Law states that citizenship in Lebanon is acquired as follows:6 * BY BIRTH: Birth within the Republic of Lebanon does not confer citizenship. * BY DESCENT: A child whose father is a citizen of Lebanon is considered to be a Lebanese citizen. A child born in Lebanon to a foreign mother, without acknowledgement by a Lebanese father, obtains the nationality of the mother. All children of Lebanese descent born outside of Lebanon must be registered at the Lebanese embassy or the child's Lebanese citizenship will not be automatically granted. * BY NATURALIZATION: Lebanese citizenship can be acquired by fulfilling the following condition: Person has applied for, and been granted, a Decree from the Lebanese Council of Ministers. Naturalized citizenship cannot otherwise be acquired.

I have also considered the evidence adduced regarding what rights a temporary residency permit confers on a person born and raised in UAE. I note from the documents7 as follows: Residence permits in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are issued through "employment or family sponsorship" on a temporary basis. UAE permits issued via employment sponsorship are issued to individuals who have been sponsored by a local company for employment purposes. Such individuals can reside and work in the UAE for a specified period of time, and, through family sponsorship, can sponsor members of their family to obtain residence permits. However, persons who acquire residence permits via family sponsorship are only able to reside in the country and are not permitted to work. Persons who have a valid UAE residence permit and are residing in the country with their parents who are also holders of valid UAE residence permits, may, upon reaching the age of 18 years, obtain a residence permit on the following conditions: - If the applicant obtains employment in the UAE, whereby the employer would obtain for the applicant, a work/residence permit - If the applicant is a student studying abroad and has presented a certificate to that affect [which has been] authenticated by [a] UAE Embassy, the parents as sponsors would be able to obtain a residence permit for their son/daughter. - If the applicant is a student studying in any UAE University in the United Arab Emirates, the parents as sponsors would be able to obtain a residence permit for their son/daughter. Residence permit holders have the right to re-enter the UAE as often as desired, provided that they do not remain out of the country for an uninterrupted period extending six months. Residence permits are cancelled when permit holders remain out of the UAE for an uninterrupted period longer than six months.

The claimant's evidence is consistent with the Response to Information Request quoted above that indicates that UAE residency permits are issued via employment sponsorship through local companies and under parental sponsorship if the potential permit holder is over the age of 18, studying abroad or studying at any UAE University in the United Arab Emirates.

The claimant's temporary residency permit expired before he left the country. He said his father was let go from his job in XXXXX 2007 and would lose his own temporary resident permit when it expired and could not sponsor him. The claimant was over the age of 18, not registered in a UAE university to obtain a university sponsorship and did not have an employer sponsor. Therefore, he did not qualify to have his permit renewed after its termination date.

The claimant has a birth certificate establishing his birth in United Arab Emirates. However, it is clear from his testimony and the documents that he does not have citizenship. Furthermore, he has been out of the country for more than six months.

I find that the claimant was not a permanent resident or citizen of UAE when he came to Canada and he made his refugee claim. He said he had only been to Lebanon for a short time when he was a little boy. His affiliation is clearly only to UAE, where he was born, educated and lived with his parents until he came to Canada. I find he is a stateless person and that his country of former habitual residence is United Arab Emirates. I also find that United Arab Emirates is the only country against which the claimant's fear of persecution will be heard. This was agreed to by the claimant's counsel at the hearing. Analysis

The determinative issue in the case now is whether there is an objective basis to the claim today and, if there is, would there be state protection for the claimant if he returned to United Arab Emirates.
Past persecution does not have to have occurred for a person to have a valid fear of persecution on return.

The claimant did not indicate that he had problems while in United Arab Emirates, except for the three interrogations about his lifelong friend who had been arrested on XXXXX XXXXX, 2007, which took place in XXXXX, XXXXX and XXXXX 2007. He said he was asked if his friend spoke of Hamas at all, and who his other friends were. The claimant said he gave no information because he had nothing to tell them. He was asked and said he did not know if any other friends or his friend's parents were questioned.

He said he felt he was followed after that. He said that after he left the country, government officials went to his parents' home on one occasion, in XXXXX or XXXXX 2007, and his parents told them he had left the country to go to school in the United States. He said that was the only time there was any enquiry.

The claimant was asked why there was not mention of UAE in his first PIF, or when he was interviewed at Immigration, and he said that he followed his first lawyer's advice. He also said he has pursued a complaint against that lawyer because of this wrong guidance.

The claimant did not exaggerate the problems he had in UAE either in his second PIF or in oral testimony. I am prepared to give him the benefit of the doubt and do not draw a negative credibility inference from his inconsistent testimony about his fears in Lebanon, as well as UAE. In any event, since I find that he is stateless and his country of former habitual residence is United Arab Emirates, I am concerned only with his fear of persecution there.

There is no evidence that he is of interest to the government today, since there have been no enquiries about him in two-and-a-half years. I find what he experienced was unfortunate but was harassment only and not persecution.

As a stateless person in United Arab Emirates, if he were to return, he would not have full rights of citizenship. I note from the 2009 US Department of State Report:8 The government registered Bidoon births but did not grant citizenship to the children. Most Bidoon lacked citizenship because they did not have the preferred tribal affiliation used to determine citizenship when the country was established. Others had entered the country, legally or illegally, in search of employment. The Bidoon faced discrimination in employment and had limited access to medical care and education. Without passports or other identity documents, their movement was restricted, both within the country and internationally.
I find the claimant would experience some discrimination in UAE, but the foregoing does not reach the threshold of persecution. Conclusion

Having considered the evidence, I find there is no objective basis to this claim. Therefore, I find that there is not a serious possibility or reasonable chance that the claimant would face persecution for a Convention ground, if he returns to United Arab Emirates, and he is not a Convention refugee.

I also considered Section 97 and determine that the claimant is not a person in need of protection, in that removal to United Arab Emirates would not subject him personally to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture for the same reasons.

Having considered all of the evidence and based on the foregoing analysis, I find the claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, not to be a Convention refugee and not to be a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.

Notwithstanding that the claim has been rejected, this is a case that may warrant humanitarian and compassionate consideration, if the claimant is unable to return to United Arab Emirates.
